extracted.intended_audience: students of English literature, literary critics, and practicing novelists
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing novels for pattern and rhythm
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and composing novels with respect to 'pattern' (shape/unity), 'rhythm' (motif/repetition and larger musical relations), and related aesthetic qualities such as atmosphere, character-construction, and the trade-offs between unity and life-like richness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern (the book's shape / unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern is an aesthetic aspect of the novel that causes us to see the book as a whole—its 'shape' or unifying design (e.g. the hour-glass, the grand chain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pattern appeals to our aesthetic sense and may be represented pictorially (e.g. Thais as an hour-glass, Roman Pictures as a grand chain). It draws most of its nourishment from the plot, externalizes atmosphere, and makes scattered incidents cohere into a single whole. Critics should not take pictorial similes literally—pattern produces a holistic pleasure often felt before it can be explained. Examples: Thais, Roman Pictures, The Ambassadors. Anti-patterns / caveats: a rigid pattern can require pruning of material and human variety, may 'shut the doors on life' and leave the novel 'beautifully done, but not worth doing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of pattern to the author's mood
rubrics_metrics.description: The chosen pattern must fit the author's mood and the tone of the work; suitability makes the pattern convincing rather than merely mechanical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roman Pictures' 'grand chain' works because the pattern matches Lubbock's comic, sub-acid, benign mood; a pattern anyone can invent is not enough—its appropriateness to the author's temperament and treatment is crucial. Evaluate whether the pattern feels natural to the mood or feels imposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as the source of pattern (plot → pattern relationship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern springs mainly out of the plot and is nourished by it; plot provides the 'carpentry' on which beauty and pattern may be built.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing pattern, trace how convergences/divergences in plot (e.g. characters' arcs, converging fates) create the overall shape. Examples: Thais (characters converge, cross, recede); The Ambassadors (symmetry created by missions from America). If the pattern feels unmotivated by plot events, it may be superficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm (easy sense: repetition plus variation / motifs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm in fiction (the 'easy' sense) is repetition plus variation—recurrent phrases, images, or motifs that stitch a work together from the inside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary rhythm can function like musical phrases (Proust's 'little phrase' of Vinteuil): recurring elements appear, fade, and return changed, giving surprise and freshness and binding disparate parts without an external shape. Well-used rhythm achieves beauty without mutilating characters. Bad rhythm hardens into a symbol (becomes boring) and trips the reader. Rhythm is often produced by local impulse rather than pre-planning; examples: Proust's use of the Vinteuil phrase. Assess recurrence, variation, and whether motifs gain a life independent of single characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm (difficult/symphonic sense: expansion and interrelation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A second, harder sense of rhythm is the large-scale, symphonic relation between major blocks of a work—an 'opening out' or expansion comparable to the whole effect of a symphony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should ask whether a novel achieves an emergent unity—something 'heard' behind the pages that wasn't literally played—by relations among large sections (analogous to movements of Beethoven's Fifth). Possible exemplars: War and Peace. This is rare and difficult to achieve; look for a sense of enlargement or liberation of parts into a larger entity rather than mere closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of recurring musical-like motifs (leitmotif / 'little phrase')
rubrics_metrics.description: The deliberate recurrence of a small, distinctive phrase or motif that travels through the text and changes meaning with context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proust's 'little phrase' from Vinteuil illustrates how a motif can be heard at different moments and thereby 'stitch' the book internally. Unlike a mere banner or symbol, an effective leitmotif can develop, change, and give orientation without being tethered to a single character or literal meaning. Evaluate how motifs change function over time and whether they provide internal cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character construction: number, range, and realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of characterisation including the number of characters, their variety, completeness, and capacity to represent the human world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rigid pattern often forces an author to limit character numbers and to 'prune' attributes (e.g. lack of stupidity, poverty, or bodily sensuality), producing types that are 'maimed' of common life (Forster's critique of Henry James). Assess whether characters are richly human, capable of variety (fun, carnality, heroism), or are deliberately curtailed to serve pattern—decide if such curtailment is justified by the aesthetic aims or is a loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of life / humanity vs. aesthetic unity (trade-off)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tension between achieving aesthetic unity (pattern) and preserving the messy richness of life and humanity in fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and critics must weigh whether the sacrifices (pruning characters, removing life-like diversities) are justified by the beauty achieved. The debate between Wells (favor life/richness) and James (favor oneness) exemplifies this trade-off. Evaluate whether unity comes at unacceptable cost to realism, empathy, or human variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmosphere as an externalized element / 'atmosphere as actor'
rubrics_metrics.description: Atmosphere (mood, setting aura) may be externalized by pattern and function almost as an actor in the novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether atmosphere is coherently sustained and whether it acts on characters and plot (e.g. 'Paris irradiates The Ambassadors'—Paris functions like an unembodied actor). Good pattern or rhythm can make atmosphere palpably operative; weak handling leaves atmosphere vague or decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-planning if aiming for rhythm (production guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm, especially the 'easy' recurrent-motif type, is difficult to achieve by rigid pre-planning and often depends on a local impulse at the right interval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For authors: do not expect to manufacture rhythmic effects by exhaustive prior plotting; effective motifs and rhythmic returns often arise organically during composition. For critics: consider whether rhythmic effects feel spontaneous or contrived. Anti-pattern: authors who plan every beat may produce stilted or symbolic repetition rather than living rhythm.
